decision.summary: The one documented mechanism cited—Loops CLI sends events and tests transactional email from the terminal—is correctly sourced (E32), and the single CTA, word count, and single-ask structure all comply with the brief. However, the draft's persuasive core rests on three material claims with no literal source support: that the editor preview doesn't trigger a real send, that the CLI needs no new integration code, and that a CLI test send exercises the template 'the same way a live event would.' These are factual assertions about product behavior, not style choices, and they are not entailed by any supplied source. 'The docs show the exact command' is plausible but unconfirmed by the captured text. Revise to either remove/soften these specific claims or supply supporting source text.

benefit_retention.explanation: The underlying mechanism—use the documented Loops CLI to send a real test transactional email from the terminal before relying on the draft—is retained and correctly sourced via E32. However, the explanatory scaffolding around it (editor-preview limitation, no-code claim, live-event equivalence) is unsupported, so the benefit is asserted more strongly than the sources establish.

brief.interpretation: Read literally: one activation email to an existing Loops user (developer) who already has an account and a draft transactional template, asking for exactly one action — send a real test transactional email to themselves. This is activation of an existing feature, not acquisition, so the CTA is not signup; it is the documented path to trigger a test send (the transactional API endpoint and/or CLI). No plan, pricing, timing, or outcome claims are needed or supported for this ask.

Selected audience (user-stated constraints): A developer with a Loops account and a draft transactional template..
No further recipient situation is established. Compiled market context is research to check for applicability, not a replacement biography.
brief.reader_profile_override: A developer with a Loops account and a draft transactional template.
brief.promise: Sending one real test transactional email to yourself is the documented way to confirm your draft template actually works before it reaches a real user.
brief.orientation: Loops is the platform that sends your product's transactional email (like receipts or password resets) from a template you build once, and you can trigger a real test send yourself from the terminal or via its API before it ever reaches a customer.
brief.arc: Single email, no sequence arc: one documented first step, one reason it matters, one destination.
brief.sequence_rationale: A single activation email can only carry one documented, checkable first step. The CLI's own description — 'test transactional email from your terminal' — and the public transactional API endpoint are the only two documented ways to trigger a real send without writing new app integration, so the brief picks the CLI path as primary (lower setup, no code required) and keeps the direct API call as a complete alternative for a developer who'd rather call it from existing code. Both route to real documentation pages rather than the registration or demo actions, which don't fit a reader who already has an account. What measurable result do customers get, and how do you know?

value_case.mechanism: The Loops CLI can send a test transactional email from the terminal, exercising the draft template the same way a live event would.
